summary: This memo defines MIB objects for managing Frame Relay interfaces on data terminal equipment, using SMIv2. It is on the standards track at draft standard status.

plainLanguage.summary: A standard set of dials for checking the connection between your equipment and a Frame Relay network.

questions: what is the frame relay dte mib
what is a dlci in frame relay
how to monitor frame relay with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP objects a router or host uses to report on its Frame Relay link, its virtual circuits and their errors.

tldr.problem: Network managers need a standard way to look at a Frame Relay connection and the many virtual circuits running over it, without every vendor inventing its own counters.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB treats a Frame Relay interface as one multi-access interface and defines three groups of objects: link management parameters, a table of circuits, and an error table, plus one trap for circuit changes.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 1315 with an SMIv2 version and is a Draft Standard that no later RFC in the unit metadata obsoletes.

today: RFC 2115 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1315, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of this Frame Relay DTE MIB as far as the record here shows.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2115 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Frame Relay interfaces on a DTE, the user-side equipment attached to a Frame Relay network. It is written in SMIv2, the second version of the Structure of Management Information.

The document sits inside the SNMPv2 management framework. RFC 1902 defines the Structure of Management Information, RFC 1213 defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects, and RFC 1905 defines the protocol used to reach those objects. Each object is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and the MIB module itself is registered as transmission 32.
sections.plainLanguage: Network gear can be asked questions with a standard list of dials and gauges. This document writes down the list for a kind of connection called Frame Relay.

sections.title: Frame Relay as One Multi-Access Interface
sections.content:
The RFC views Frame Relay as a multi-access medium, not as a group of point-to-point connections. There is a single interface to the network (the physical connection) with many destinations, which are the virtual connections. Grouping all virtual connections under their physical connection is meant to make diagnostics and troubleshooting simpler.

The interfaces MIB would allow each Frame Relay data link connection to be its own interface with its own ifTable entry. The RFC says this is not recommended and is not directly supported, and that with demand circuits it is not possible to create an entry for each one.

To tie circuits to a higher layer, the circuit table has two index fields, frCircuitIfIndex and frCircuitLogicalIfIndex. In the RFC's example, DLCIs 20 and 30 run IP directly on interface 2, while DLCIs 40, 41 and 42 use interface 2 as frCircuitIfIndex but point to a proprietary protocol layer (interface 3) as their logical interface.

The RFC also lists how generic interface objects should be read for Frame Relay. ifType is frameRelay (32), ifMtu is the maximum frame size in octets, and ifSpeed is the access rate, which can differ from the speed of the physical interface underneath. ifInBroadcastPkts and ifOutBroadcastPkts are always zero because there are no broadcast frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of one big building entrance with many hallways. You count the people at the entrance, but you can also count them in each hallway, and you can label a few hallways as belonging to the same club.

sections.title: Link Management Parameters
sections.content:
The first group describes the Data Link Connection Management Interface (DLCMI), the signalling that reports which virtual circuits exist. The table frDlcmiTable has one row per interface, indexed by frDlcmiIfIndex.

frDlcmiState says which management scheme is active, with values such as noLmiConfigured (1), lmiRev1 (2), ansiT1617D (3), ansiT1617B (4), itut933A (5) and ansiT1617D1994 (6). frDlcmiAddress gives the address format (Q.921, two Q.922 variants, or the final Q.922), and frDlcmiAddressLen is two, three or four octets.

Several timers and counters follow ANSI T1.617 Annex D. The polling interval is 5 to 30 seconds (default 10), the full-enquiry interval is 1 to 255 polls (default 6), the error threshold is 1 to 10 (default 3), and monitored events is 1 to 10 (default 4). If the station sees the error-threshold number of errors within the monitored-events number of intervals, the interface is marked as down.

Other objects cover the maximum number of virtual circuits, whether multicast service is in use (frDlcmiMulticast), the interface state (frDlcmiStatus: running, fault or initializing) and a RowStatus for creating rows.
sections.plainLanguage: This part holds the settings for how your equipment keeps checking in with the network, such as how often it asks, and how many missed answers it allows before it decides the line is down.

sections.title: The Circuit Table
sections.content:
The frCircuitTable describes each DLCI (Data Link Connection Identifier) layered onto a Frame Relay interface. It is indexed by frCircuitIfIndex and frCircuitDlci. The management virtual circuit, DLCI 0, counts as a circuit and has its own row.

The DLCI textual convention is an Integer32 from 0 to 8388607. The description says interfaces normally use 0..1023 but may be configured for ranges as large as 0..2^23.

Each row holds state, counters and traffic parameters:

  • frCircuitState is invalid, active or inactive. The invalid value is deprecated in favour of frCircuitRowStatus.
  • Counters track frames and octets sent and received, FECN and BECN congestion indications, discard-eligible (DE) frames in each direction and discarded inbound frames.
  • frCircuitCommittedBurst, frCircuitExcessBurst and frCircuitThroughput describe the traffic contract. When committed burst and throughput are both non-zero, the measurement interval is committed burst divided by throughput.
  • frCircuitMulticast is unicast, oneWay, twoWay or nWay, and frCircuitType is static or dynamic.
sections.plainLanguage: Each hallway gets its own report card. It says whether the hallway is open, how many people went through, and how much traffic the hallway was promised.

sections.title: The Error Table
sections.content:
The frErrTable has one row per Frame Relay interface and records the last error seen. frErrType names the kind of error, frErrData holds as much of the offending frame as possible (1 to 1600 octets, and at minimum the Q.922 address or as much as was delivered), and frErrTime records when it happened using sysUpTime.

Two objects were added in this version: frErrFaults counts how many times the interface has gone down since initialization, and frErrFaultTime records when it was last taken down for exceeding the error threshold.

Under the compliance statement, the error group is optional and is described as used for debugging Frame Relay systems.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the equipment keeps a note of what kind of mistake it was, a copy of the bad message and the time, like a teacher writing down the last thing that went wrong.

sections.title: Traps and Conformance
sections.content:
Virtual circuits are added, deleted and change availability during normal operation. The MIB defines one trap, frDLCIStatusChange, meant as a companion to the SNMP Link Up and Link Down traps. It reports a circuit that was created, invalidated, or toggled between active and inactive. If the cause is the DLCMI going down, per-DLCI traps should not be generated.

Two objects control it. frTrapState is enabled or disabled and defaults to disabled. frTrapMaxRate is the number of milliseconds that must pass between traps, 0 to 3600000, with a default of 0 (no minimum). If events come faster, an implementation may skip traps or queue them.

Conformance is defined by two module compliances, frCompliance and frCompliance0. In frCompliance the port and circuit groups are mandatory, while the error, trap and notification groups are optional, and row creation is not required for the DLCMI and circuit tables.
sections.plainLanguage: The equipment can ring a bell when a hallway opens or closes. By default the bell is switched off, and you can say how long it must wait between rings so it does not get annoying.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1315
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 1315. The main change is converting the module from SMIv1 to SMIv2; because of that, table indices are read-only instead of not-accessible. The module name changed from RFC1315-MIB to FRAME-RELAY-DTE-MIB.

Objects were added to the DLCMI table (frDlcmiStatus, frDlcmiRowStatus), to the circuit table (for example frCircuitMulticast, frCircuitType, frCircuitDiscards, frCircuitLogicalIfIndex and frCircuitRowStatus) and to the error table (frErrFaults, frErrFaultTime), along with frTrapMaxRate. New enumeration values itut933A (5) and ansiT1617D1994 (6) were added to frDlcmiState. Object groups and module compliances were created.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of the checklist. It uses newer wording rules and adds extra questions people found they needed.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The RFC says security issues for this MIB are entirely covered by the SNMP Security Architecture and have not been expanded within the MIB. It adds nothing of its own here.

Some objects can be changed (for example the DLCMI parameters and trap settings are read-write or read-create), so whoever can write to them through SNMP is controlled by that SNMP security machinery.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules about who may look at or change the dials come from the general network management system, not from this document.

items.label: receiveLong
items.desc: Frame exceeded the configured maximum length.

items.label: illegalAddress
items.desc: Address field did not match the configured format.

items.label: unknownAddress
items.desc: Frame on a circuit that was not active or was disabled.

items.label: dlcmiProtoErr
items.desc: Unspecified error interpreting a link maintenance frame.

items.label: dlcmiUnknownIE
items.desc: Information Element not valid for the configured protocol.

items.label: dlcmiSequenceErr
items.desc: Unexpected sequence number in a link maintenance frame.

items.label: dlcmiUnknownRpt
items.desc: Report Type Information Element not valid.

items.label: noErrorSinceReset
items.desc: No errors since the last cold or warm start.

viz.caption: THE THREE GROUPS OF THE MIB

items.title: DLCMI
items.text: Link management parameters for each interface.

items.title: Circuits
items.text: One row per virtual circuit, with state, counters and traffic parameters.

items.title: Errors
items.text: The last error seen on each interface, plus fault counts.
